qs.q: Why could yeast alone not turn rice into alcohol?
o: Because rice contains starch and yeast cannot eat starch
Because rice contains too much sugar
qs.e: Rice contains no sugar, so it cannot have too much. Yeast does not need grapes: sugar dissolved in water is enough. Acidity is not the issue.

qs.q: Why does a brewer add neutral distilled alcohol before filtration?
o: To extract flavours trapped in the rice solids
To turn the sake into a spirit
qs.e: Sake stays a fermented drink and is later diluted with water. The alcohol does not restart fermentation and adds no colour: it is neutral.

qs.q: What colour are the middle layers of a rice grain?
qs.e: Brown is the colour of the outer layers, which are nearly always removed. Neither green nor black describes any part of the grain.

qs.q: Why is the rice turned regularly by hand during the initial mould growth?
o: So that the mould grows evenly
qs.e: The mould is wanted, not removed. Yeast comes in at fermentation, and kōji is never taken below freezing.

qs.q: In nearly all sake styles, which ingredient contributes most to the aromas?
qs.e: In many styles rice, kōji and water give relatively little flavour. Added alcohol is neutral: it helps extract flavour but brings none of its own.

qs.q: What does nihon-shu, one of sake's official names, literally mean?
qs.e: 'Pure rice' is the meaning of junmai, a label term. 'Big' recalls the dai in daiginjō. No official name means 'fine rice wine'.

qs.q: Which four stages turn brown rice into steamed white rice?
qs.e: Malting, milling and mashing belong to beer. Sake rice is neither germinated nor roasted.

qs.q: Which combination usually produces a fruity, floral sake with little acidity and umami?
o: Highly polished rice, special yeasts, cool fermentation
Lightly polished rice, special yeasts, ageing
Highly polished rice, warm fermentation, no filtration
qs.e: Lightly polished rice and warm fermentation give cereal, lactic notes with more acidity and umami. Filtration is required by law anyway.

qs.q: What does daiginjō literally mean?
qs.e: 'Pure rice' is junmai and 'aged sake' is koshu. Nama (unpasteurised) is sometimes described as 'raw', but that is not daiginjō.

qs.q: A label shows 純米吟醸. What does it indicate?
o: Junmai ginjō: fruity style, no added alcohol
Honjōzō: cereal style, with added alcohol
Daiginjō: with added alcohol, rice at 50%
qs.e: There is no 本醸造 (honjōzō) and no 大 (dai). Futsū-shu does not carry these premium terms.

qs.q: What aromas can a nama quickly develop?
qs.e: Flowers and pear are ginjō notes, not linked to nama. Vanilla and coconut come from oak, which is hardly used for sake.

qs.q: Which of these sakes has no added distilled alcohol at all?
qs.e: Daiginjō, ginjō and honjōzō without the word junmai are sakes with alcohol added before filtration.

qs.q: A label reads 純米大吟醸. What is in the bottle?
o: Junmai daiginjō: rice at 50% or less, no added alcohol
Daiginjō: rice at 50% or less, with added alcohol
Junmai ginjō: rice at 60% or less, no added alcohol
Honjōzō: rice at 70% or less, with added alcohol
qs.e: Without 純米 it would be a daiginjō with added alcohol; without 大, a junmai ginjō. Honjōzō is written 本醸造.

qs.q: Which two speciality styles, together in one bottle, give a cloudy sake with bubbles?
qs.e: Nama only means unpasteurised and koshu aged: neither makes a sake cloudy or fizzy.

qs.q: A sake is polished to 45% with no added alcohol. What is the highest grade it can carry?
qs.e: Daiginjō and honjōzō mean added alcohol. Junmai ginjō would be possible, but it is not the highest grade for rice at 45%.

qs.q: Which kanji means 'big' and tells a daiginjō from a ginjō on a label?
qs.e: 純 is the jun of junmai; 本 and 造 are the first and last kanji of honjōzō.

qs.q: Why is it usually spelled nama-zake rather than nama-sake?
o: In Japanese the 's' softens to a 'z' in this word
Zake is a different drink, made from barley
It is the name of the region of origin
qs.e: Zake is neither another drink nor a place, and aged sake is called koshu.

qs.q: Which production step is legally controlled for junmai?
qs.e: No pasteurisation defines nama, ageing defines koshu, and rough filtration defines nigori.

qs.q: In which term does the kanji 米 (mai) appear?
qs.e: Ginjō (吟醸), honjōzō (本醸造) and daiginjō (大吟醸) do not contain 米.

qs.q: Besides dried fruit and nuts, which aromas can a typical koshu show?
qs.e: Vanilla and coconut come from oak, which is very rarely used for sake. The other notes do not describe an aged sake.

qs.q: How many kanji must you learn to recognise the four key label terms?
qs.e: Writing out the four terms takes ten symbols in all; but jō appears three times and gin twice, so there are only seven different symbols.

qs.q: What is assessed under 'appearance' when tasting?
qs.e: Sweetness, acidity, umami and finish are judged on the palate; aroma families on the nose (and palate).

qs.q: How should sake bottles be stored?
qs.e: Lying bottles down is a habit for cork-sealed wine, not sake.

qs.q: What is the recommended serving temperature for ginjō styles?
qs.e: Heat would flatten the fruity, floral scents. Below freezing the sake would be too cold to smell.

qs.q: Why pair delicate sashimi with a light sake?
o: So food and sake have a similar flavour intensity
Because light sake is always more expensive
Because fish only goes with warm sake
qs.e: Price, temperature and strength are not the reason for this advice.
